summary.text: A joint distribution gives the probability that two or more random variables land in particular ranges or sets of values together.
With exactly two variables it is called bivariate, and from it you can work out each variable's marginal distribution and the conditional distributions.
In a table for two draws, each inner cell holds the probability of one combination of results, and all the cells together sum to 1.

steps.text: A table shows the probability of each combination of results for A and B.
To get the chance of A alone, add the cells across every possible result for B.
Those sums are written in the margin of the table.
So the margin shows the chance of A only when B takes one particular value.

paragraphs.heading: Several variables at once
paragraphs.text: When several random variables, say X and Y, are defined on the same probability space, their joint distribution gives the probability that each one falls in whatever range or set of values you pick for it. With just two variables it is called a bivariate distribution. The same idea works for any number of variables.

paragraphs.heading: Ways to write it down
paragraphs.text: A joint distribution can be described by a joint cumulative distribution function. It can also be given by a joint probability density function when the variables are continuous, or a joint probability mass function when they are discrete. From these you can get two other kinds of distribution. The marginal distribution gives the probabilities for one variable with no reference to the others. The conditional distribution gives the probabilities for some variables once the rest are fixed at particular values.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a table
paragraphs.text: Picture a table for two draws, A and B. Each of the four inner cells holds the probability of one combination of results, and together those cells are the joint distribution. Because the draws are independent, each cell is the probability of A's result times the probability of B's result. The four cells add up to 1, as every probability distribution must. The last row and last column give the marginal distributions of A and B; for example, the chance that A is red, whatever B turns out to be, is 2/3, written in the margin.

paragraphs.heading: A die example
paragraphs.text: Roll a fair die. Let A be 1 if the number is even (2, 4 or 6) and 0 otherwise, and let B be 1 if the number is prime (2, 3 or 5) and 0 otherwise. The joint probability mass function of A and B gives a probability for each pair of outcomes. These probabilities must add up to 1, since some combination of A and B is certain to happen.

paragraphs.heading: When variables are independent
paragraphs.text: Two discrete random variables X and Y are independent exactly when, for every x and y, the chance that X = x and Y = y together equals P(X = x) times P(Y = y). For continuous variables the test is the same with densities: for all x and y, the joint density f_(X,Y)(x, y) must equal f_X(x) times f_Y(y). In plain terms, learning something about one variable leaves the distribution of the others just as it was. None of them tells you anything about the others.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring how they move together
paragraphs.text: It is often useful to measure how two variables vary together. A common measure is the covariance, which tracks a linear relationship and may miss a relationship that is not linear. The correlation scales the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations, so it has no units and can compare pairs of variables measured in different units. If the points of the joint distribution that have positive probability tend to lie along a rising line, the correlation is near +1; along a falling line, near −1. A correlation of exactly +1 or −1 means those points lie exactly on a straight line.
